claims.text: Lattice distortion is the primary mechanism governing enhanced hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Random mixing of multiple elements with different atomic radii produces severe lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation motion.
HEAs with greater atomic-size mismatch have better mechanical properties than compositionally similar alloys with lower mismatch.
The intended initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase HEA with a random elemental distribution, such as a refractory BCC HEA.
Substituting constituent elements with elements of more similar atomic radii will reduce atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion consists of variations in interatomic distances and bond lengths caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Distortion from differently sized atoms acts as a barrier to dislocation motion and raises the applied stress required for plastic deformation.
The increased stress required for plastic deformation results in increased hardness and strength.
The higher-mismatch HEA will have significantly higher hardness and yield strength than the reduced-mismatch HEA.
An equimolar HEA provides the maximal expected atomic-size mismatch among its constituents.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to single-phase BCC or FCC HEA solid solutions.
The hypothesis should hold when secondary-phase precipitation is below 5 vol.%.
Precipitation, carbides, or oxides can provide additional strengthening that obscures or dominates lattice-distortion strengthening.
A NbMoCrTiAl-based composite containing about 7.0 vol.% Al2O3 and 32.2 vol.% TiC had approximately 50% greater compressive fracture strength than the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA.
Failure to observe a statistically significant decrease in both hardness and yield strength after reducing atomic-size mismatch would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field calls the reduced-mismatch modified HEA the baseline, whereas the baseline and falsification fields define the high-mismatch HEA as the baseline.
